characterizations.result_summary: FTIR spectroscopy was used to confirm the chemical structure of synthesized poly(amide-urea)s, with characteristic peaks reported in Table 1.

1H-NMR spectroscopy was used to confirm the chemical structure of the synthesized poly(amide-urea)s, with the characteristic appearance of urea linkages and disappearance of amine linkages observed in spectra.
Mn of the synthesized poly(amide-urea)s ranges from 14200 to 22000, Mw ranges from 35700 to 48500, and dispersity (Mw/Mn) ranges from 2.20 to 2.51.
Measured glass transition temperatures of 8 poly(amide-urea) samples, confirmed DMTA Tg results, no melting endotherm observed for all tested samples.
Measured initial thermal decomposition temperature (T_i), 10% weight loss temperature (T_10) and maximum decomposition temperature (T_max) for 8 polyurea samples, data listed in Table 3.
All tested polyurea polymers are amorphous
The tested poly(amide-urea)s had absorption maxima at 303–429 nm assignable to the Q Q<sup>-</sup> transition resulting from the conjugation between the aromatic rings and nitrogen atoms.
Inherent viscosities of poly(amide-urea)s were measured.

Thus, two series of poly(amide-urea)s were prepared via the polyaddition reactions of four different diisocyanates (aromatic, semi-aromatic, and cycloaliphatic) including PPDI, NDI, 4,4 -diphenyl methane diisocyanate (MDI), and H<sub>12</sub>MDI with the prepared diamines at $7 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$for 4 hr (Scheme 2).

The temperatures for 2% gravimetric loss (T ) of the polyureas were about 192–2298C, and the temperatures for 10% gravimetric loss $( T _ { 1 0 } )$that are important criteria for the evaluation of thermal stability were in the range of $2 8 5 { - } 3 2 7 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$and also the char yields of polymers at 7008C were about 36–49%.

In the polymers derived from the same diamine and different diisocyanates, PPDI-derived polyurea showed the highest thermal stability, likely related to the fully aromatic and more symmetric structure of this polymer, whereas $\mathrm { H } _ { 1 2 } \mathrm { M D I }$-derived polyurea showed the lowest thermal stability, probably due to its weak aliphatic linkages.

Also, from the diamine point of view, 1AQA-derived polymers from the same diisocyanate reveal higher thermal stability in comparison with 2AQAderived polymers due to the more symmetric, better growth of molecular weight, and close packing of polymer chain.

Thermal behavior of the polymers was studied using dynamic mechanical thermal analysis (DMTA). By increasing the temperature from 30 to $3 0 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C }$, one transition was seen for the polymers at which tan d went through a maximum. This transition was related to the glass transition temperature of the polymers. Also DSC analysis confirmed data obtained from DMTA. The glass transition temperature $( T _ { \mathrm { g } } )$was taken as the midpoint of the change in the slope of the baseline. Also, no polymer showed a clear melting endotherm which resulted from the amorphous nature of the polymers. The glass transition temperature of 1AQA-PPDI was higher than 1AQA-MDI due to the more rigidity of PPDI with respect to MDI structure.

A round-bottomed flask equipped with an $\Nu _ { 2 }$inlet tube, condenser, and thermometer was charged with 0.005 mol of diamine and 10 ml of dry NMP. Then a solution containing 0.005 mol of diisocyanate in 10 ml of dry NMP was added in one lot to the flask contents. The solution was stirred for 1 hr at room temperature and 4 hr at $7 0 ^ { \circ } \mathrm { C } ,$and then it was precipitated in water.
